title: Marquinhos’ magnificent block stopped Liverpool’s comeback before it even started
content:
But can they do it on a wet and cold Tuesday night at Anfield?

This wasn’t the beautiful game as Paris Saint-Germain know it. Forget “trying to create superiority in every part of the pitch” — the mantra of their coach Luis Enrique. For 72 minutes, in the wind and driving rain and against a Liverpool team who were fighting to save their season, it was all about a block. Not a low block, nor a mid block, but an old school put-your-body-on-the-line-type block.

There were 30 minutes on the clock when Virgil van Dijk’s eyes lit up. The PSG goal was yawning invitingly in front of the Liverpool captain following Matvei Safonov’s sprawling one-handed save to deny Milos Kerkez. Time seemed to stand still as Van Dijk stepped forward in the six-yard box and swung his left boot at the ball. For context, his shot had an xG of 0.84.

This was the early breakthrough that Liverpool craved, an opportunity to shake PSG’s belief and to send the home supporters into a frenzy in a stadium that had been a cauldron of noise since kick-off. In short, it was game-on territory.

Marquinhos, the longest-serving player in PSG’s history, has form for what happened next, both in terms of his heroic last-ditch defending and his reaction.

In September 2014, during a 3-2 victory over Barcelona, the Brazilian threw himself in the way of a close-range Jordi Alba shot, blocked the effort brilliantly and celebrated wildly after the ball was deflected behind. Alba walked off in disbelief, holding his head in his hands.

Five years later, Marquinhos was chest-bumping Thiago Silva, his countryman and mentor at PSG, after forcing Mohamed Salah to run the ball out of play at the Parc des Princes for Liverpool.

They were moments that stayed in the mind and helped to shape and define Marquinhos’ image in a PSG shirt, in particular in the eyes of their supporters, who embraced and admired the central defender’s passion and commitment.

But they were also moments that, in the context of those European campaigns, didn’t matter one jot. PSG were serial failures in the Champions League during that era and Marquinhos was part of that story, including the notorious defeat in the Nou Camp in 2017, when a 4-0 first-leg victory was thrown away in humiliating fashion. For all their domestic success, PSG kept coming up short in the competition that really mattered.

That narrative changed spectacularly last season, when PSG emerged as the outstanding team in Europe and Marquinhos, who has played in a variety of positions for the club, including midfield, led them to a 5-0 triumph against Inter in the Champions League final.

Signed from Roma in 2013 at the age of 19, in the early stages of the Qatar Sports Investments era, Marquinhos has been there, seen it and done it at PSG, making over 500 appearances. In fact, there must be times when he looks at the photos on the walls, thinks about all the players who have come and gone — more than 100 signings — and feels like the last man standing.

“I feel old!” Marquinhos said in an interview with CBS Sports after this 2-0 win at Liverpool, when he was asked how it feels to be surrounded by so many younger players now.

At Anfield, Marquinhos was the first man sitting rather than the last man standing — in his case, sitting in the six-yard box with his legs outstretched and both fists clenched while he let out a roar.

Lunging in desperation, his left boot connected with the ball a split-second after Van Dijk made contact — a goal-saving challenge if ever there was one — and a release of energy and emotion followed, as well as a kiss from his goalkeeper.

“For a defender, moments like that are better than scoring a goal. It’s what I enjoy most!” Marquinhos told Canal+ afterwards. “I saw Van Dijk arriving and had the reflex to throw myself at the ball. These are the details that change a game.”

Or, in the case of the second leg at Anfield, the details that kept the game the same (goalless on the night and 2-0 on aggregate) and denied Liverpool the lead that would have given them real hope.

This was an entirely different game from the first leg at the Parc des Princes, where Liverpool played what their head coach Arne Slot acknowledged as “survival mode” football to try to contain the European champions.

The numbers were turned around at Anfield — literally in some cases. Seventy-four per cent possession for PSG in Paris became 47 per cent in Liverpool. PSG made 29 clearances in the second leg — more than twice as many as Liverpool — and faced 21 shots compared to three in Paris.

It wasn’t exactly backs-to-the-wall for PSG, but there were moments, in particular in the first 25 minutes of the second half, when Luis Enrique’s players had to show resilience as Liverpool turned up the pressure.

“We knew that we would be suffering at times,” Luis Enrique said.

Willian Pacho, playing alongside Marquinhos in central defence, was impressive, even if he was only a VAR intervention away from giving away a penalty. Slot could have kicked up a fuss about that afterwards. Instead, he pointed out that good fortune had been smiling on his players in Paris last week. Full marks for honesty.

Luis Enrique was no different in his tone, with the PSG coach admitting that Liverpool deserved a goal.

Instead, though, it was his team who scored again, and it was a goal of the highest quality in the way that it was constructed.

A lovely interchange midway inside the PSG half saw Ousmane Dembele allow a pass from Achraf Hakimi to run through his legs. Khvicha Kvaratskhelia was standing behind him, waiting to receive before offloading to Dembele, who ran into the space that opened up before curling a ball into the path of Bradley Barcola.

With Liverpool stretched, Kvaratskhelia and Dembele combined again, the latter coolly placing a left-footed shot beyond the reach of Giorgi Mamardashvili for the first of his two goals.

It was another left foot, though, belonging to Marquinhos, that gave PSG the platform for a victory that takes them into the last four for the third year running.
